summary:
No measure specific to Rize concerning transgender visitors appears in the sourced material. What a trans visitor faces in the province is the national framework of Turkey, applied in full.

That framework is moving toward criminalisation without the prohibitions yet being law. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Reform package would pave the way for criminal charges against LGBT people, describing it as one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades; on 28 October 2025 activists held a press conference in Istanbul against its provisions targeting LGBT people. Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people made public during 2025, an assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain. None of the three was submitted to parliament.

Criminalisation remains prospective rather than statutory. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a visitor refused service, stopped or harmed on those grounds has no statutory prohibition to invoke.

Public assembly is where state force is applied most visibly. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were continuing at the end of the year. Istanbul illustrates a national pattern rather than an isolated episode, since pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans.

Transition-related care is restricted. In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency, under the Ministry of Health, banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.

The legislative position kept shifting after that. The draft judicial package considered in 2026 had its LGBTI-discriminatory provisions removed. A press report of February 2026 described a proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison, and that proposal was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill, the 12th judicial package.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, which matters for couples travelling together on evidence of their relationship, and it removes one route by which a visitor might establish a recognised partnership in an emergency.

The legislative environment is unsettled in both directions. Three separate draft packages targeting LGBTI people were published in 2025, the discriminatory provisions of the following year's draft package were stripped out, and a further proposal appeared in February 2026 before failing to reach the omnibus bill. A visitor reading Turkish law at any given moment may be reading text that is about to change.

International monitoring bodies record the trajectory as a coordinated rollback rather than scattered incidents. Human Rights Watch characterised the leaked October 2025 package as among the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades, while Amnesty International described the three packages of 2025 collectively as an unprecedented assault on LGBTI rights in the country.
localsOnly:
Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are assessed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof to substantiate the declaration, and risk their resulting 'unfit report' being leaked publicly.

Legal gender recognition has existed since 1988, so the procedure is available to residents; the sourced material does not set out its requirements, and the 2025 draft packages would have made recognition nearly impossible to obtain had they been enacted.

Absent a comprehensive anti-discrimination statute, residents have no national legal instrument prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, which leaves complaints dependent on general criminal and civil provisions.

In December an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images on social media that were incompatible with 'society's moral values' and could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. The judgment shows a provincial court willing to close an LGBTI organisation on moral-grounds reasoning.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three draft packages published in 2025 was subsequently enacted, and whether the February 2026 proposal advanced beyond the press report, is unresolved in the sourced material.

No Rize-specific or regional source addresses police conduct, local Pride activity, detention practice or healthcare access in the province, so the assessment rests entirely on the national framework without province-level corroboration.

The scope of the June 2025 hormone restriction is not stated beyond the under-21 age threshold. Whether adults over 21 face any additional prescribing barrier, in Rize or elsewhere, is not sourced.

The reasons behind the removal of the LGBTI-discriminatory provisions from the 2026 draft package, and whether they may return in a later bill, are not documented.
